2. It is stated in the petition that the petitioner is a private Limited liability Company incorporated on 9th August, 1963 for the purpose of, inter-alia, manufacture of ceramic bricks, clinkers and refractory and mechanised brick products. The petitioner obtained gas connection in respect of its two brick-fields as per two separate contracts made between the Respondent No. 1 and the petitioner on 19.5.80 for a period of 4 years under Customers Nos. 330002 and 3380004 respectively. Subsequently, these contracts were renewed for another period of 4 years entered into on 12.12.86. All on a sudden the Respondent No. 1 issued two letters being letter Nos. 3380004 and 3380002 dated 8.11.88 and received on 14.11.88 intimating that as per the Respondent No. 2's order natural gas should not be supplied to the petitioner any more. No reasons or grounds have been stated in the said letter and in fact, on 15.11.88 the Respondent No. 1 disconnected the gas connection in respect of Gas Customer No. 3380004. That the said orders are arbitrary, capricious and whimsical and disconnection in respect of the line will result in colossal loss to the petitioner and the public at large resulting in shortage of materials in the market, high price and corruption and the order is liable to be cancelled/ rescinded and/or withdrawn as these are made without lawful authority. It is also stated that the order of the Respondent No. 1 is contrary to fundamental rights which guarantee fair play in business and other trade. 

 3. An affidavit-in-opposition has been filed by the Respondent No. 1 wherein it is stated that the Respondent No.1 is not a person performing any function in connection with the affairs of the Republic or a local authority and bears no resemblance to the recognised concept of a 'Local authority' and it is a public limited liability company entrusted with the conduct of certain affairs appertaining to Titas Gas Transmission and Distribution and as such, the Writ petition is not maintainable in law. It is further stated in the affidavit-in-opposition that Article 102 of the Constitution is not meant for enforcing a contract or for preventing a breach of contract and since the claim is founded on a contract, writ petition does not lie to enforce the performance, or to restrain the breach, of a contractual obligation and as such, the Rule is liable to be discharged. 

 4. It is further stated that the petitioner having failed to point out any violation of any statutory rule or law or any malafide on the part of the Respondent No.1 in disconnecting the gas unit line No. 3380004 the relief sought for is not amenable to writ jurisdiction. It is also stated in the affidavit-in-opposition that the statements made in paragraph No.19 of the writ petition are misleading, motivated and not correct. It is stated that the impugned notices, Annexure 'P' and 'P(1)', were issued for violation of a contractual obligation and also to implement the decision of the Government to stop natural gas to the consumers who are using gas for the purpose of manufacturing common bricks. There were two gas units being Unit No. 3380002 and 3380004 for using gas in the brick-fields of the petitioner. The first unit No. 3380002 was industrial Unit for manufacturing Ceramic and refractory bricks. Subsequently, the second Unit being No. 3380004 was opened as a seasonal one and ultimately raised to the status of an industrial unit for manufacturing common bricks which is now prohibited by the recent decision of the Government of Bangladesh. Though the impugned notice, Annexure 'P' to the writ petition, was issued for the first unit being No. 3380002 on 8.11.88, it was not implemented and the gas line of the petitioner in respect of the first unit i.e. No. 3380002 was not disconnected. Since the second unit gas line being No. 3380004 was used to manufacture common bricks which is prohibited by the Government decision, the respondent No. 1 issued the impugned notice Annexure 'P(1)' to the Writ petition to carry out the decision and to implement it as directed by the Government vide letter No. 8/Petro-2(27)/88/2106 dated 3.11.88 issued by the Respondent No. 2 and the after disconnected the gas line in respect of the second unit No. 3380004. It is denied that the impugned notices are arbitrary, capricious, whimsical and that disconnection in respect of one line being No.3380004 will result in colossal loss to the petitioner and the public at large resulting in shortage of materials in the market or that the impugned orders were made without lawful authority. The Respondent No. 1 acted lawfully, rightly and legally in accordance with the decision of the Government in order to implement the prohibition order for using the natural gas for the purpose of manufacturing common bricks by the consumers. It is further stated in the affidavit- in-opposition at paragraph 22 that the statements made in paragraph 27 of the Writ petition are misleading, motivated and not wholly correct. It is stated that according to the decision of the Government (vide Annexure-1) the use of natural gas was strictly prohibited for the purpose of manufacturing common bricks, by the concerned manufacturers and for that reason the impugned notices were issued by the Respondent No. 1. But as a matter of fact, natural gas line of Unit No. 3380002 was not disconnected since the unit was not for manufacturing common bricks within the meaning of the Government decision. 

 5. An affidavit-in-opposition was also filed by the Respondent No. 2. In that affidavit-in-opposition it is stated at paragraph No. 12 that the statements made in paragraph No.19 of the Writ petition are misconceived and misleading and incorrect and hence, denied by this deponent. It is further stated that the impugned Annexure 'P' and 'P(1)' were issued for implementation of the Government decision against the common brick manufacturers and that the Government decision is applicable for the 2nd gas unit No. 3380004 of the petitioner, which manufactures common bricks for use as mortar. In respect of gas unit No. 1 (3380002) the petitioner's company found that it was manufacturing ceramic and other special types of bricks. So, the notice debarring the petitioner from manufacturing ceramic bricks and other special types of bricks through its first unit was issued through in advertance and has not been acted upon. It is further stated that the first unit of gas line will continue if the petitioner does not manufacture ordinary bricks through this unit. The second unit gas line was for manufacturing ordinary bricks, so it was disconnected on 15.11.88 as per Government decision. The said decision was taken by the Government for the greater cause of the nation and to ensure gas supply to the vital industrial units like fertilizer factories and power stations; gas supply was prohibited for the manufacture of common bricks. The petitioner has no vested right to get preferential treatment and privilege to use gas in manufacturing common bricks. The said decision of the Government has been annexed to the affidavit-in-opposition of the Respondent No. 1. It was further stated that the Government has taken decision to discontinue supply of gas to common brick manufactures as a matter of policy without any discrimination. 

 11. Mr. Nazmul Huda, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the Respondent No.1, raised a preliminary question as to the maintainability of the Writ petition arguing that it is not maintainable as the Respondent No.1 is not performing any function in connection with the affairs of the Republic. He has further argued that the Respondent No. 1 is not a person and as such, no relief can be sought against the Respondent No. 1 in the Writ jurisdiction of this court. Mr. Hasan Ali, the learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing for the State, in addition to the stands taken by Mr. Nazmul Huda, has also raised the question of maintainability of the Writ petition as against the Respondent No. 1 and, according to him, as the petitioner is not a 'person' he has no locus standi to file an application under Article 102 of the Constitution. 

 12. In reply, Mr. Asrarul Hossain has argued that the petitioner being a juristic person must be deemed to be a "person" within the meaning of Article 102 of the Constitution. He has also referred us to para 7 of the Supplementary Affidavit-in-opposition filed by the Respondent No. 1 wherein it is stated that by operation of law the Respondent No. 1 which was previously a private limited company was brought under the control of the Bangladesh Oil and Gas Corporation which is a statutory corporation and also the Ministry of Mineral, Oil and Gas Resources, Government of Bangladesh. He has also referred to the Bangladesh Petroleum Act, 1974 and Section 2 of the General Clauses Act and submitted that the Respondent No. 1 is a "local authority" and as such, Article 102 of the Constitution is available as a remedy against any act done by it. 

 "That it is stated that the respondent No. 1 is a public liability limited company established long before the liberation of Bangladesh and by operation of law the respondent No. 1 was brought under the control of Bangladesh Mineral, Oil and Gas Corporation. The respondent No. 1 has no statutory power to do or not to do something since the respondent No. 1 is controlled and guided by the Bangladesh Mineral, Oil and Gas Corporation and the Ministry of Mineral, Oil and Gas Resources, Govt. of Bangladesh." 

 19. In this Act "petroleum" is defined in section 2 (e) (i) as any naturally occurring hydrocarbon, whether in a gaseous, liquid or solid state. So, the Government in exercise of the sovereign powers of the state has the exclusive right to sell and distribute natural gas and for performing this function the Respondent No. 1 has been functioning under the control and supervision of, and as a subordinate functionary, of a statutory corporation that is, the Bangladesh Oil and Gas Corporation. Under Clause (5) of the Article 102 "a statutory public authority" is a "person" within the meaning of the said Article. The Bangladesh Oil and Gas Corporation is undisputedly a statutory public authority established under section 2(b) of the Bangladesh Petroleum Act. 1974 and as such, it is a 'person' within the meaning of Article 102 and the Respondent No. 1 being a subsidiary of this parent Corporation is attracted within the jurisdiction of Article 102 of the Constitution. 

 24. Mr. Nazmul Huda and Mr. A.F. Hasan Arif next contend that the petitioner having sought enforcement of a purely contractual obligation against the Respondent No. 1, the petition is not maintainable as Article 102 of the Constitution is not available for enforcement of a contract and is meant for vindication of a specific legal right. In support of their contention they have placed reliance on a number of decisions namely, Radhakrishan Agarwal and others Vs. State of Bihar and others reported in AIR 1977(SC)1946, Divisional Forest Officer Vs. Bishwanath Tea Co. Ltd; reported in AIR 1981(SC)1368. The Bihar Eastern Gangetic Fishermen's Co-operative Society Ltd. Vs. Sipahi Singh and others reported in AIR 1977 (SC) 2149, Mis Munin Motor Vs. The Regional Transport Authority reported in PLD 1962, 108, Purba Nanda Das Vs. Executive Engineer, Relief and Rehabilitation reported in AIR 1961 Assam 101 and Talekhal Fishermen's Co-operative Society V s. Bangladesh BLD(AD) 1981, 103. 

 26. In Radhakrishna Agarwal and others Vs. State of Bihar and others, AIR 1977(SC) 1496, it was held that in order to come to a decision if facts were required to be investigated and if those facts were disputed no relief would be granted under the writ jurisdiction. In that case the question of a contractual obligation not arising out of any statutory power or obligation was involved. 

 32. In the case, S.M.S. Samity Vs. Bangladesh 39 DLR (AD) 85 relied upon by Mr. Asrarul Hossain all the above decisions were considered and distinction was made between an (1) ordinary contract and (2) a contract in exercise of a statutory or executive or sovereign power of the state. It was then held that a contract assuming the characteristics of the latter class is enforceable by the court in its writ jurisdiction. In the cited case; it was found that provisions had been made for leasing out fisheries and lands by the Government under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, and various rules were framed thereunder for entering into contract of lease and when the petitioner sought to enforce by writ petition such a contract of lease of a fishery given to it but subsequently cancelled and then given to another person, it was held that the said contract having been entered into by the Government in performance of its functions under statutory rules was enforceable by the court in its writ jurisdiction. In this connection, the following observations of their Lordships must be quoted:- 

 33. In the present case, it has already been observed that the State is the owner of natural gas in its sovereign capacity by dint of a constitutional provision i.e. Article 143 of the Constitution and the Government is empowered to explore, distribute, sell etc. this wealth under the Bangladesh Petroleum Act, 1974. There is, therefore, no doubt that the Respondent No. 1 entered into a contract with the petitioner for supplying this wealth as a subsidiary of the Government authorised to exercise Government's power to deal with this wealth. As such, the contract in this case was not an ordinary contract like "supply of charirs" and was not entered into by the Respondent No. 1 acting in the "Trading capacity" and discharging an ordinary trading function of the Government. It was, on the other hand, a contract necessitated for performing the function of the state as a sovereign power and arising out of statutory rules. As such, respectfully following the principles enunciated in the above case, we are of the view that although the relief sought for in this petition arises out of a con-tract, the petition is maintainable.
